Boson. Bosons are particles with integer spin—zero, one, two, and so on—that obey Bose-Einstein statistics, allowing multiple identical particles to occupy the same quantum state. The Standard Model includes fundamental gauge bosons like photons, W and Z bosons, and gluons that mediate forces, as well as the Higgs boson that generates mass. Composite bosons like pions and mesons emerge from quark interactions.

Unlike fermions, bosons are not subject to the Pauli exclusion principle, so unlimited numbers of identical particles can exist in one quantum state. The fundamental bosons include gauge bosons, which are force mediators, and the Higgs boson. Composite bosons include mesons, glueballs, and systems capable of Bose-Einstein condensation.

Bosons are the universe's force-carrying mediators. The photon, a massless spin-one boson, is responsible for electromagnetism and makes light itself. The W and Z bosons are massive weak force carriers, while gluons mediate the strong force. The discovery of massive gauge bosons validated the electroweak unification, while the Higgs boson, discovered in two thousand twelve, confirmed the mechanism by which particles acquire mass. Bose-Einstein condensation demonstrates quantum coherence at macroscopic scales. Photons are the massless electromagnetic boson, gluons are the massless strong-force boson, and mesons form composite bosons alongside their fermionic partners.
